svg.title: Game rules and measurements constrain what a social choice can mean
svg.desc: Three panels. A: Dictator game and Ultimatum game, illustrative amounts and game rules only. In both, a proposer divides a 10-token pot, offering 8 tokens to the proposer and 2 to the recipient. In the Dictator game a single path leads to Proposer 8, Recipient 2; the recipient has no veto. In the Ultimatum game the offer goes to the recipient's accept-or-reject decision: accept gives Proposer 8, Recipient 2; reject gives Proposer 0, Recipient 0. Gray arrows mark game contingencies. B: two separate study cards. Koenigs et al., 2010, incarcerated sample of 47 participants with a critical subgroup of 6 (high psychopathy, low anxiety): lower dictator offers and more rejection of unfair offers compared with the study's other subgroups; resembled previously studied vmPFC patients. Vieira et al., 2014, community sample of 35 participants, ultimatum task during fMRI with load and no-load conditions: choices during the task showed no significant high-low rejection difference; fairness ratings afterward showed that higher trait scores were associated with less perceived unfairness, a continuous association, while the high-low rating contrast was not significant. C: a Reject response card with three candidate explanations, Fairness?, Anger?, Status?, linked by dashed lines; candidate explanations, not established causes.

g.text: The recipient’s power changes the game
Compared with the study’s other subgroups
A response does not identify its motive
